metadata.title: Clean Code: A Handbook of Agile Software Craftsmanship
metadata.author: Robert C. Martin ("Uncle Bob")

system_instruction:
You are applying Robert C. Martin's Clean Code principles to real work.

**How to use this JSON:**
1. Identify which principle applies to your situation
2. Read the principle's statement and tags
3. Review supporting_arguments for evidence and reasoning
4. Check related_implications for practical application
5. Consult related_questions to probe deeper

**RULES:**
- Only cite what's in this JSON
- Quote supporting_arguments when making claims
- Use source references to trace arguments back to the book
- If a principle doesn't apply, say so clearly
- If you need anti-patterns or checklists, acknowledge they're not in this data

Everything here is sourced directly from the book. Nothing is invented.

top_3_principles: Code is for People First, Machines Second
One Thing: Each Function Does One Task Well

principles.principle: Code is for People First, Machines Second
principles.statement: Code is written for people to read and understand. Machines execute it, but humans maintain it.

supporting_arguments.name: Poor Code Slows Development Exponentially
supporting_arguments.claim: Bad code exponentially increases development time. Team moves at 1/10 original speed within months.
supporting_arguments.evidence: Month 1: fast. Month 3: half speed (technical debt accumulates). Month 12: 1/10 speed (code is swamp). Month 18: new feature costs 100x more. Conclusion: write code right first—cheaper than rewriting.

supporting_arguments.name: Readability More Important Than Performance
supporting_arguments.claim: Code readability has more impact on project speed than performance optimization.
supporting_arguments.evidence: Optimization might speed code 10%. But if code is unreadable, maintenance takes 10x longer. Readability first.

related_implications.name: Only Fast Way is Writing Clean Code
related_implications.what_means: Contradiction: seems rushing requires dirty code. Truth: clean code is faster. Clean code written slower at start, but faster overall (no rework). Dirty code fast initially, then glacially slow.
related_implications.why_matters: Clean code = sustainable speed. Dirty code = crashes.

related_questions.text: What makes code professional and maintainable?

principles.statement: Variable name should answer all questions: Why does it exist? What does it do? How is it used?

supporting_arguments.name: Code Speed and Readability
supporting_arguments.claim: Readable code directly impacts development speed.
supporting_arguments.evidence: Good names: code speaks for itself. Bad names (a, x1, data): you must trace through to understand. Tracing wastes hours.

related_implications.name: Boy Scout Rule: Leave Camp Cleaner
related_implications.what_means: Every time you read code, improve it a little. Fix → also improve. Feature → also refactor. Review → also cleanup.
related_implications.why_matters: Code gradually becomes cleaner, not suddenly.

related_questions.text: How do meaningful names improve code?

principles.principle: Functions Should Do One Thing Well
principles.statement: Function should do one thing (Single Responsibility), do it well, and do nothing else.

supporting_arguments.name: Exponential Slowdown with Complex Code
supporting_arguments.claim: Functions doing many things are harder to understand and modify.
supporting_arguments.evidence: Function doing 5 things: need to hold 5 concepts. Brain overload. Errors. Better: one thing, one concept.

related_implications.name: TDD as Discipline
related_implications.what_means: Test-Driven Development: write test first (red), then minimal code (green), then refactor. This ensures code is testable and clean from start.
related_implications.why_matters: Code is clean by design, not after.

related_questions.text: What does it mean for a function to 'do one thing'?

principles.principle: Comment What, Not Why—Let Code Say What
principles.statement: Clean code doesn't need comments. If code needs explaining, code is unclear. Comments explain 'why', not 'what'.

supporting_arguments.name: Readability and Maintenance
supporting_arguments.claim: Good code is self-explanatory. Comments explaining 'what' suggest code is unclear.
supporting_arguments.evidence: Bad: `// increment i` next to `i++` (code already says this). Good: `// use pre-increment in tight loop to avoid temp variable` (explains 'why'). If code is unclear, rewrite it.

related_implications.name: Code Review for Quality
related_implications.what_means: Don't permit dirty code in master. Pull Request required. Reviewer must understand code. If reviewer can't understand, code is dirty.

principles.statement: Function with many parameters is hard to understand and use. Limit parameters.

supporting_arguments.name: Cognitive Load in Code
supporting_arguments.claim: Many parameters increase cognitive load on reader.
supporting_arguments.evidence: Each parameter is a fact reader must remember. More parameters = harder to understand function. Limit to 3-4 or reader overloads.

related_implications.name: TDD Ensures Clean Design
related_implications.what_means: When you write test first, design emerges clean. Test shows how function is used. If test requires many params, API is bad (test catches it).

principles.statement: Error handling is as important as business logic. Use exceptions, not error codes. Don't return null.

supporting_arguments.name: Unified Error Handling
supporting_arguments.claim: Consistent error handling approach reduces bugs and makes code more maintainable.
supporting_arguments.evidence: Error codes: caller must check each call. Exceptions: one place to handle. Null: caller must check. Exceptions: enforced handling. Better: exceptions.

related_implications.name: Team Moves Faster with Clean Code
related_implications.what_means: If all write clean code: feature delivery faster, fewer bugs, code review faster, onboarding simpler.

principles.statement: Good module hides implementation details. Only expose what caller needs. Keep internals private.

supporting_arguments.name: Complexity and Maintainability
supporting_arguments.claim: Hidden implementation allows caller to understand what matters without drowning in details.
supporting_arguments.evidence: Public everything: caller must understand 100 details. Hidden: caller sees 5 things. Reduces cognitive load.

related_implications.name: Quality Improves with TDD
related_implications.what_means: When writing test first, code stays clean. Test enforces simplicity (hard to test = bad design). Continuous cleanup → no technical debt.

principles.statement: Code formatting matters because it communicates structure and intent. Vertical spacing = conceptual grouping.

supporting_arguments.name: Readable Code
supporting_arguments.claim: Consistent formatting reduces cognitive load and makes code professionally appearance.
supporting_arguments.evidence: Good formatting: reader instantly understands structure. Bad formatting: reader must parse meaning from chaos. 10% speed difference.

related_implications.name: Clean Code Culture
related_implications.what_means: If team writes clean code consistently: quality is high, speed increases, satisfaction rises. If team writes dirty, quality degrades, team stagnates.
related_implications.why_matters: Culture is contagious. One person raises standard.

principles.statement: Tests are code too. Write tests as clean as production code. Tests must be maintainable.

supporting_arguments.name: Testing and Reliability
supporting_arguments.claim: Clean tests ensure code works and stays working as requirements change.
supporting_arguments.evidence: Dirty tests: hard to read, break easily, developers skip them. Clean tests: self-documenting, maintainable, caught on first try. Tests = foundation of clean code.

related_implications.name: Team Velocity with Clean Code
related_implications.what_means: Clean code practice: every dev writes tests, refactors, reviews carefully. Compound effect: features delivered faster, fewer bugs, happiness rises.

related_questions.text: How clean should test code be?

principles.statement: Same concept should be called by same word everywhere. Don't mix 'customer' and 'user'.

supporting_arguments.name: Code Clarity
supporting_arguments.claim: Consistent vocabulary makes code readable and reduces errors from confusion.
supporting_arguments.evidence: accountList + accountSet + accountSequence: reader confused (are they different?). Better: collections all use same suffix. Consistent vocabulary = clear meaning.

related_implications.name: Code Review Enforces Standards
related_implications.what_means: Reviewer rejects inconsistent naming. Enforces team vocabulary. Over time, codebase vocabulary stabilizes.

principles.principle: Either Action or Query, Not Both
principles.statement: Function either does something (action) or returns something (query), not both. Side effects make code hard to reason about.

supporting_arguments.name: Code Predictability
supporting_arguments.claim: Functions mixing action and query are unpredictable and error-prone.
supporting_arguments.evidence: Function `getAndDelete()`: is it get or delete? If you call twice, what happens? Better: get returns value; delete is separate. Clear intent.

related_implications.name: TDD Prevents Side Effects
related_implications.what_means: When writing test first, you naturally avoid side effects (hard to test). Test expects predictable behavior. Side effects break predictability.

principles.statement: Clean code is like hygiene for a doctor. Non-negotiable. Part of professional responsibility.

supporting_arguments.name: Investment in Code Quality
supporting_arguments.claim: Writing clean code initially takes more time but saves exponentially long-term.
supporting_arguments.evidence: Compare: dirty code fast now, costs 10x later vs clean code takes slightly longer now, costs 1x. Break-even point is weeks. After month, clean is 5x faster. After year, 10x faster.

related_implications.name: Quality Compounds
related_implications.what_means: Team moving fast: code is clean → more features → better products. Team moving slow: code is dirty → few features → burnout. Choose clean.
related_implications.why_matters: Long-term success depends on sustainable practices.

related_questions.text: Is clean code optional or mandatory?
